source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in LLMs but disappeared in ChatGPT
finding: Older GPT-3 models fall for CRT traps like people do. ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 mostly do not.
numbers: 10 OpenAI models, temp 0; 150 CRT items (3 types x 50) plus 50 semantic illusions; humans n=455 (500 recruited, 45 excluded). CRT intuitive-answer rate: davinci-003 80%, humans 55%, ChatGPT-3.5 15%, GPT-4 0%. Correct: davinci-003 5%, humans 38%, ChatGPT-3.5 59%, GPT-4 96%.
limits: Human CRT 38% vs 41% in original (n=3428). Items may be memorised. OpenAI models only. Authors say RLHF or exposure explanations are untested.
agent_relevance: The fast-and-wrong failure belongs to a model generation, not to LLMs in general. Test our base model on CRT-style traps before adding any System 2 scaffold.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) same paper, Study 2 prompt manipulations
finding: A one-line suffix that triggers step-by-step work moves an old model from intuitive to correct. Forbidding step-by-step work hurts only the stronger model.
numbers: davinci-003 with 'Let's use algebra': chain-of-thought 0%->100%, correct 5%->28%, intuitive 80%->29%. ChatGPT-3.5 told to answer briefly: CoT 97%->0%, correct unchanged (P=0.49). GPT-4 told briefly: CoT 84%->0%, correct 95%->88%, intuitive 0%->10%.
limits: Single suffix wording per condition. CRT only.
agent_relevance: The fast/slow switch in an LLM is largely a prompt-triggered output style (write intermediate steps or not). A cheap code-controlled toggle.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) same paper, Studies 3-5 few-shot and instruction fixes
finding: Examples and a check-assumptions cue repair intuitive errors in an old model, so the error is a prompt-sensitive habit.
numbers: davinci-003 few-shot CRT: type 2 2%->92% after 2 examples; type 3 12%->92% after 7; type 1 0%->78% after 30. Semantic illusions: 'check the question for invalid assumptions' suffix raised correct 18%->54%, intuitive 72%->28%. Semantic illusion correct: ChatGPT-3.5 74%, GPT-4 88%.
limits: Gains are for one model and schematic items; may be pattern learning, not reasoning.
agent_relevance: A short warning cue is a cheap alternative to a full deliberation pass on trap-prone problems.

source: Binz & Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 gave the intuitive wrong answer on all three CRT items. It looked human on vignettes but small rewordings broke it.
numbers: CRT1-3: 3 of 3 intuitive answers. 12 vignette problems: 6 correct, all 12 human-like (right answer or human-type error). Cab problem with 15%/85% base rates could be pushed to very different answers by small edits. 13,000+ decisions-from-description problems: only the largest model (davinci) near human regret. 3 of 6 Kahneman-Tversky biases reproduced (framing, certainty, overweighting).
limits: Original GPT-3 only (2022). Authors note training contamination for famous vignettes.
agent_relevance: Famous-paradigm success can be memorisation. Use perturbed items when we test any deliberation operator.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Models, like people, reason better when the content agrees with their beliefs. This is a belief-bias analogue.
numbers: Three tasks: NLI, syllogism validity, Wason selection. NLI: high accuracy for humans and models, little content effect. Syllogisms and Wason: lower accuracy and clear content advantages in both. On Wason, models exceed humans in accuracy and in size of content effect. Few-shot gave mild gains and did not remove content effects.
limits: Mostly pre-instruction-tuned models (Chinchilla family). No chain-of-thought condition in the main results.
agent_relevance: Belief bias is present in the base model. A check that strips content (abstract the variables) is a justified conflict-detection operator for logic items.

source: Weston & Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention (is something you might need too)
finding: Ask the model to first rewrite the input keeping only relevant, unopinionated text, then answer from the rewrite. This removes sycophancy and distractor effects.
numbers: LLaMA-2-70B-chat factual QA with opinion in prompt: baseline 62.8%, oracle (no opinion) 82.0%, S2A 80.3%. Long-form objectivity +57.4%. GSM-IC irrelevant sentences: 51.7%->61.3% with S2A (about +12 points random, +10 in-topic distractors). Instruction 'ignore irrelevant text' gave no consistent gain.
limits: One model family; GPT-4 grades factuality (200 prompts). Extra inference pass costs tokens.
agent_relevance: A concrete S1-to-S2 operator: context cleaning before solving. Matches G4/G5 (keep opinions and proposed answers out of the solver).

source: Yu et al. (2024) Distilling System 2 into System 1
finding: Slow multi-step methods can be compiled into fast one-shot answers for some tasks but not for multi-step arithmetic.
numbers: Last-letter task: Llama-2-70B-chat zero-shot 30.0%, 2-step Rephrase-and-Respond 44.5%, distilled direct answer 98.0% (about 25 tokens). TriviaQA with biased opinion: System 1 51.6%, S2A 76.0%, distilled S2A 81.3%. GSM8k: System 1 zero-shot 9.40%, CoT zero-shot 36.39%, distilled CoT 7.13% (distillation fails; teacher targets only 56.81% accurate).
limits: Needs weight training, which our scaffold-only agent cannot do.
agent_relevance: Learn which problem classes need System 2 (arithmetic chains yes; bias and distractor cleaning less so) and spend deliberation only there.

source: Su et al. (2025) Dualformer: controllable fast and slow thinking by randomized reasoning traces
finding: One model trained on randomly truncated reasoning traces can run in fast, slow or auto mode.
numbers: 30x30 maze: slow mode 97.6% optimal vs 93.3% for full-trace baseline with 45.5% fewer steps; fast mode 80% vs 30% for solution-only; auto mode 96.6% optimal with 59.9% fewer steps. Fast mode found 42 unique feasible paths vs 3. MATH fine-tuning (Mistral-7B): slow greedy +1.7 points at p=0.1.
limits: Needs training; maze and Sokoban are synthetic with A* traces. Math gains small.
agent_relevance: Mode choice can be a controlled variable. For us, mode must be set by code from a signal, not by the model.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: a generative agent with fast and slow thinking
finding: Agent loop built on dual process: a small trained model acts by default and a large LLM is called only when a code rule fires.
numbers: ScienceWorld, 30 task types, 270 variations: SwiftSage 84.7 vs SayCan 33.8, ReAct 36.4, Reflexion 45.3. Tokens per action: SayCan 1,855.84, ReAct 1,971.03, Reflexion 2,983.46, SwiftSage 757.07. Swift is flan-t5-large (770M) tuned on 62k oracle actions.
limits: Textual simulator only. Fast module needs oracle trajectories. Baselines adapted by the authors.
agent_relevance: Closest working precedent for our S0 gate and G1: default cheap path, escalate on signal.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage, switching rule
finding: The switch from fast to slow is four code-checked conditions, not a model judgement. After slow planning, a buffer of about 5 actions runs before returning to fast.
numbers: Switch to SAGE when: (1) stuck, 5 consecutive steps with zero reward; (2) invalid predicted action; (3) critical decision such as final answer; (4) unexpected observation. SAGE uses two LLM calls producing an action buffer.
limits: Rules tuned to ScienceWorld rewards.
agent_relevance: Maps onto our impasse detector. The critical-decision trigger is a useful extra: always verify before the final answer.

source: Christakopoulou et al. (2024) Agents thinking fast and slow: a Talker-Reasoner architecture
finding: Splits a conversational agent into a fast Talker and a slow Reasoner that updates shared state.
numbers: Architecture paper with a sleep-coaching example. No benchmark numbers reported. Claims modularity and lower latency.
limits: Position paper, no controlled test. I read the abstract and introduction only.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. Do not cite as support for a performance gain.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse
finding: Chain-of-thought hurts on tasks where verbal deliberation also hurts people: implicit pattern learning, face recognition, rules with exceptions.
numbers: Artificial grammar learning (440-problem subset): o1-preview 36.3 points below GPT-4o zero-shot; CoT drops 23.1 (GPT-4o), 8.0 (Claude 3 Opus), 6.05 (Gemini), 8.8 (Llama 3.1 70B). Face recognition: all 6 vision-language models worse with CoT. Exceptions-rule task: CoT needed up to 331% more rounds. Logical-inconsistency, spatial intuition and working-memory tasks: mixed or no harm.
limits: The human-to-model mapping failed in 3 of 6 tasks, where models had priors or memory that humans lack.
agent_relevance: Supports G11. A human finding (deliberation can hurt) predicted where an LLM gets worse, so keep a no-deliberation arm for pattern and perception tasks.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: Across 100+ papers and 20 datasets with 14 models, CoT gains concentrate on math and formal logic.
numbers: GSM8K gain up to 66.9 points, MATH up to 41.6; commonsense, language understanding and reading comprehension show little or no gain. On MMLU, CoT matches direct answering unless the question or response contains an equals sign. Free-form BiGGen Bench: only mild gain. A symbolic solver beats CoT.
limits: Zero-shot CoT focus. Gains vary by model.
agent_relevance: A gate rule: deliberate when the class is symbolic or arithmetic, answer directly otherwise. Code-checkable cue (equals sign, numbers).

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: o1-like models spend huge token budgets on trivial questions with almost no accuracy gain.
numbers: On '2 plus 3' o1-like models used on average 1,953% more tokens than conventional models; one case produced 13 solutions. Self-training that removes redundant solutions cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 for QwQ-32B-Preview with accuracy kept.
limits: Math benchmarks only; open o1-like models.
agent_relevance: Quantifies the cost of always-slow. Backs G11/G12 (spend by difficulty).

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Exploring the System 1 thinking capability of large reasoning models (S1-Bench)
finding: Reasoning models over-think on easy questions and sometimes get them wrong. They notice this looks simple but still think long.
numbers: 422 simple questions (220 English, 202 Chinese, avg 14.46 tokens), 28 LRMs. Closed-source LRMs use over 3x the tokens of small non-reasoning models. Weak LRMs under 90% pass@1: instruction-following 76.7%, knowledge 78.6%, reasoning 88.1%. 18 of 23 LRMs did not shorten answers when they called the question easy. LaserD-1.5B and AdaptThink-1.5B cut AIME tokens about 50% but only about 25% on S1-Bench; AutoThink-1.5B reached 60.1% accuracy there.
limits: Items built to be model-simple; length-reduction methods tested were small distilled models.
agent_relevance: The model's own it-is-easy remark is not a reliable switch. Use an external difficulty signal (G12).

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse scaling in test-time compute
finding: Giving reasoning models more thinking tokens lowers accuracy on some tasks. Failure modes differ by model.
numbers: Four task categories, five failure modes: Claude models get more distracted by irrelevant info with longer reasoning; OpenAI o-series resist distractors but overfit to familiar framings; models drift from sensible priors to spurious features (few-shot examples largely fix this); all models lose focus on constraint-tracking deduction (zebra puzzles); Claude Sonnet 4 shows more self-preservation statements at longer reasoning.
limits: Constructed tasks designed to expose failures. Not typical workloads.
agent_relevance: Direct support for capped thinking length (G11) and for few-shot anchoring when a model drifts.

source: Ma, Xie et al. (2025) Do large language models truly grasp mathematics? Modified CRT
finding: Change the CRT item so the old trick no longer works. Models still use the old trick, as an intuitive reflex would.
numbers: 5 LLMs on 50 CRT3 items. Number-change types: A average 86.8%, B 68.5%, C 53.1%, algebra version D 20.9%. Experiment II (changed principle): original 99.1%, modified 1.5% average; 95.9% of errors reused the old method. Original CRT2 Claude 3 62.0%->22.0%. o1-preview on modified items: 10.0% average, 82.5% of its errors repeated the original answer. Human accuracy fell only 14% in Exp II.
limits: Small human sample (5 lab researchers, each answered 20% of items). Modified items may be ambiguous. Reading errors as System 1 is the authors' interpretation.
agent_relevance: Strong test for a conflict-detection step: does this problem differ from the familiar one? Build a perturbation check with a held-out variant (G3).

source: Beucler, Purcell, Charles, Desender & De Neys (2025) Computational modeling of heuristic base-rate integration (CCN abstract)
finding: A conflict-detection lab uses LLMs to measure how strongly a heuristic pulls on base-rate problems.
numbers: 151 human participants, continuous base-rate task. LLM results were cut off in the search snippet; not read.
limits: Seen in a search snippet only.
agent_relevance: Possible human-versus-LLM calibration of heuristic pull. Open the PDF in a later pass.

source: Franssens & De Neys (2009), critique of response-time evidence for conflict detection (via search snippet)
finding: Part of the human conflict-detection effect on response time may come from extreme base rates, not from logical intuition.
numbers: No figures read. Snippet says the response-time increase for stereotypical answers was fully mediated by extreme probabilities.
limits: Search snippet only; attribution of the critique to this paper not verified.
agent_relevance: Warns that a lab effect we copy as a conflict signal may be a stimulus artifact. Verify before use.

source: Li et al. (2025) DynamicMind: a tri-mode thinking system for LLMs
finding: A prompt-based Fast / Normal / Slow system with a small router. The default normal mode is often best.
numbers: On GSM8K, 80.52% of samples were handled more efficiently in normal mode than in fast or slow mode. Fast mode saved 599 tokens vs normal on one commonsense item. Slow mode helped 3.11% of tasks (+53.84% accuracy on those) at about 233 extra tokens. Router transfer between Qwen and Llama changed accuracy by 0.3 to 6 points.
limits: Router trained on a self-built dataset (TMC). Modes are prompts, so effects are model-specific. I read abstract, introduction and results text, not the full paper.
agent_relevance: Slow mode pays off for a small share of items. Prior for our gate: slow helps rarely, so trigger it on signal.

source: Cheng et al. (2025) Incentivizing dual process thinking for efficient LLM reasoning (ACPO)
finding: Reinforcement learning with explicit fast/slow tokens and a difficulty-based token budget cuts redundant reasoning.
numbers: AIME 2024: ACPO-1.5B 30.0% with 6,670 tokens vs 16,894 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (60.5% fewer). Another benchmark: 1.5B tokens 643->572 with accuracy 79.9%->81.3%; 7B 88.3% at 413 tokens. MATH: 1,679 tokens vs 3,098 for GRPO, with GRPO slightly more accurate.
limits: Needs verifiable data; trained small models; authors state limits for open-domain tasks.
agent_relevance: Confirms difficulty-aware budgets work when training is allowed. Our code-side analogue: per-problem budget (G12).

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: deliberate problem solving with LLMs
finding: A deliberate search layer (propose thoughts, evaluate, backtrack) on top of left-to-right generation, framed as System 2 over System 1.
numbers: Game of 24: GPT-4 chain-of-thought solved 4% of tasks; Tree of Thoughts solved 74%. Also tested on Creative Writing and 5x5 Crosswords.
limits: Large token cost; the model also scores its own thoughts, which G5 distrusts. Gains on search-shaped tasks only.
agent_relevance: Evidence for search over single-pass reasoning where a foothold exists (G12). Replace the model's own scoring by code checks.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage, why LLM-only baselines fail
finding: Baselines that call the LLM every step repeat meaningless actions when something unexpected happens.
numbers: SayCan and ReAct need a new LLM call each time step; ReAct and Reflexion need human-written subgoal examples per task type. Reflexion beat ReAct on short tasks only.
limits: Qualitative author account.
agent_relevance: Supports escalation on impasse, not constant deliberation.

source: Weston & Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention, ablations
finding: Keeping the original text next to the cleaned text weakens the fix. Single-step S2A is only slightly worse than two-step.
numbers: Factual QA with opinions: S2A 80.3%; variant keeping original context 74.5%; a prompt-only variant 71.7% (from 62.8% baseline) with sycophancy remaining (Refute Correct 38% vs oracle 82%).
limits: Same set as main result; GPT-4 grader.
agent_relevance: When we clean context, the solver must not see the original. Matches G5.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) content effects paper, response-time link
finding: Model answer probabilities line up with human response times, as if both find the same items hard.
numbers: Item-level analyses on NLI and syllogisms found significant association with human response time. Humans who took longest on Wason did better, mainly on realistic versions.
limits: Correlational. Time spent is not the same as System 2.
agent_relevance: Model confidence on an item may serve as a free difficulty signal, a candidate for the S0 gate. Test it.

source: Chen et al. (2025) overthinking paper, process-level finding
finding: Extra solutions after the first correct one add little and repeat the same strategy.
numbers: Authors report three patterns across math benchmarks: extra solutions contribute minimally to accuracy, lack diversity of strategy, and occur more often on simple problems. Tested on GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME.
limits: Descriptive analysis of open model families.
agent_relevance: Cap the number of self-checks after a first passing check; further rethinking is wasted.
